claims.text: The conventional W–Cu reference composite has a randomly distributed tungsten phase in a copper matrix.
Directional solidification can create an engineered, continuous tungsten network interpenetrating the copper phase.
Templated infiltration can create an engineered, continuous tungsten network interpenetrating the copper phase.
The proposed improvement is intended to hold under high-temperature, high-heat-flux irradiation conditions typical of fusion-reactor joints.
A connected tungsten network provides continuous thermal-conduction pathways.
The surrounding copper phase maintains structural support in the network composite.
The surrounding copper phase provides energy absorption under irradiation.
The continuous tungsten network reduces thermal resistance.
The continuous network creates direct, connected paths for electron and phonon transport.
The connected electron and phonon transport paths increase the composite's thermal conductivity.
Tungsten has sufficient inherent mechanical strength to preserve the durability of the engineered composite.
Tungsten has sufficient inherent irradiation stability to preserve resistance to irradiation-induced defects.
The engineered composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable conventional W–Cu composite.
The thermal-conductivity improvement will involve minimal or no loss of mechanical strength.
The thermal-conductivity improvement will involve minimal or no loss of irradiation resistance.
A random, discontinuous tungsten distribution produces suboptimal thermal-conduction paths.
Significant processing defects or incomplete tungsten connectivity can prevent the predicted benefits.
Controlled neutron and gamma irradiation can replicate the relevant fusion-reactor irradiation environment for the comparison.
